items.title: Vertical Farming for Climate Resilience
items.partnerLine: UNDP Jordan and the Royal Scientific Society · Funded by Sida
items.location: Jerash, Mafraq and the Jordan Valley
items.challenge: Water scarcity and limited growing space make reliable local production difficult in several Jordanian communities.
items.solution: iPlant deployed smart vertical farming units with integrated controller technology under “Scaling up Water Innovation for Climate Security”.
items.result: The project demonstrated consistent controlled crop production with reduced water demand across multiple Jordanian sites.

items.title: iGROW
items.challenge: Urban agriculture needs to make better use of water, energy and underused city spaces.
items.solution: iPlant contributed hydroponic systems and control technology to an integrated model combining growing, solar energy, greywater treatment and rainwater harvesting.
items.result: The project demonstrated how multiple resource systems can work together in an urban sustainability model.

items.title: CEA Research Room
items.challenge: Researchers need repeatable growing conditions for year-round trials and environmental studies.
items.solution: iPlant built a climate-controlled indoor farming environment with monitored lighting, irrigation and environmental conditions.
items.result: The facility supports controlled plant trials and academic research throughout the year.

items.title: Urban Green Roof
items.challenge: Rooftops across Amman sit unused while the city absorbs heat and imports most of its fresh produce.
items.solution: iPlant built a productive rooftop for leafy greens at an agricultural education centre, doubling as a teaching space.
items.result: The roof produces food where it is eaten, reduces heat absorbed by the building, and demonstrates rooftop farming to students and visitors.

systems.title: Systems
systems.headline: Growing systems for space, climate and resources.
systems.intro: iPlant designs and builds controlled growing systems that suit the environment they are deployed in — from compact indoor units to rooftop production and the control layer that runs them.

hug.title: HUG
hug.headline: Controlled growing, at room scale.
hug.intro: HUG is a compact indoor growing system designed for hospitality, workplace, education and residential settings. It manages irrigation, lighting and climate automatically, so fresh herbs and leafy greens can be grown where they are used.

points.title: Where it fits
points.body: Restaurants, hotels, offices, schools and homes — anywhere fresh produce is used and space is limited.

points.title: What it grows
points.body: Herbs and leafy greens on a continuous cycle, harvested at the point of use.

points.title: How it runs
points.body: Irrigation, lighting and climate are managed automatically and monitored by the iPlant controller.

points.title: How it is supplied
points.body: Available outright or through Farming as a Service, where iPlant operates and maintains the system.

greenspin.title: GREENSPIN
greenspin.headline: Vertical growing that follows the sun.
greenspin.intro: GREENSPIN combines vertical farming with the MENA region’s abundant daylight. A rotating carousel moves trays through the growing cycle while water and nutrients recirculate, increasing productive area without relying on rows of artificial grow lights.

points.title: Use natural daylight
points.body: The rotating structure gives crops more even access to available sunlight and reduces dependence on artificial grow lighting.

points.title: Move every tray through the cycle
points.body: Carousel movement carries each tray through the growing system in a controlled, repeatable sequence.

points.title: Recirculate water and nutrients
points.body: Water and nutrients return through the system instead of being used once and discarded.

points.title: Grow more in a compact footprint
points.body: Vertical arrangement multiplies productive growing area and can be paired with solar power for suitable sites.

rooftop.title: Productive Rooftop Farming
rooftop.headline: Unused roof area, turned productive.
rooftop.intro: Productive Rooftop Farming brings food production to roof space that is otherwise doing nothing. Systems are specified for hot, dry conditions, with irrigation designed around real rooftop exposure rather than ideal growing conditions.
rooftop.note: This is a growing system and service. iRoof — the modular green-roof tile product — is separate and has its own website.

points.title: Where it applies
points.body: Commercial, institutional and residential rooftops with usable load capacity.

points.title: Climate-adapted design
points.body: Irrigation and crop selection specified for heat, exposure and water limits.

points.title: Local food production
points.body: Produce grown at the point of consumption, reducing transport and handling.

points.title: Integrated with control
points.body: Can run under the same monitoring layer as iPlant's indoor systems.

automation.title: Smart Controllers, Automation & AI
automation.headline: One control layer across every system.
automation.intro: iPlant's controllers monitor and manage irrigation, lighting, climate and nutrient delivery. Conditions are measured continuously and held against target ranges, with remote visibility of how each system is running.

points.title: Monitoring
points.body: Temperature, humidity and system conditions measured continuously at the growing plane.

points.title: Automation
points.body: Irrigation, nutrient dosing, lighting and ventilation managed against target ranges.

points.title: Remote visibility
points.body: System status is visible without needing to be on site.

points.title: Deployed in the field
points.body: The same control technology runs across research rooms, vertical farms and indoor units.

points.title: AI-assisted optimisation
points.body: Measured conditions feed decision-making that tunes irrigation, lighting and climate toward the target range, with image-based diagnostics in development.

faas.title: Farming as a Service
faas.headline: Fresh growing, fully managed.
faas.intro: Farming as a Service removes the operational burden of running a growing system. iPlant installs the unit, monitors it remotely, supplies nutrients and seedlings, maintains the hardware and harvests on a schedule.

how.title: Assess
how.body: We look at the space, the produce needed and how the system will be used day to day.

how.title: Install
how.body: iPlant delivers and commissions the unit, and sets the growing schedule.

how.title: Operate
how.body: Conditions are monitored remotely, with nutrients and seedlings supplied on cycle.

how.title: Harvest
how.body: Scheduled harvesting and service visits keep production continuous.

benefits.heading: Why controlled growing works better.
benefits.description: Water, seasons, space and consistency are designed into the system instead of being left to chance.

items.title: Use water more precisely.
items.body: Recirculating hydroponic systems deliver water and nutrients directly to the root zone, reducing avoidable losses compared with open soil irrigation.

items.title: Grow beyond the season.
items.body: Controlled lighting, irrigation and environmental conditions support more consistent production through heat, cold and changing outdoor weather.

items.title: Harvest where food is used.
items.body: Restaurants, hotels and workplaces can harvest fresh herbs and greens close to the kitchen, improving freshness, consistency and presentation.

items.title: Make every square metre productive.
items.body: Vertical, indoor and rooftop formats turn constrained or overlooked spaces into organized growing areas without requiring conventional farmland.

items.title: Replace guesswork with visibility.
items.body: Sensors, controllers and remote monitoring help manage irrigation, lighting and environmental conditions while reducing the burden on the operator.

items.title: Produce locally, with less dependence.
items.body: Systems are designed around local climate, water, space and operational needs, helping cities build more resilient and shorter food-production chains.

uplift.headline: What would control and light add?
uplift.intro: Most greenhouses in the region stop producing twice a year — once to summer heat, once to winter cold and short days. Holding the climate and topping up the light closes both gaps.
